Case 1 · S1 Corporation

AI Video Surveillance Platform

Security operators pieced investigations together across many screens. I redesigned the journey from finding a person to tracking their movements and reporting the incident as one continuous workflow, and used AI-built prototypes to align every team before development began.

My role
  • Led UX strategy and information architecture
  • Built AI prototypes and ran early validation
Team
2 designers · 3 engineers · 1 PM
Timeline
Jun – Sep 2026
Platform
Desktop web app
Tags
B2BSearchAI prototypingEnd-to-end
Outcome

From a fragmented tracking process to one continuous flow

Detail-page visits to find a person
avg. 50
A preview panel keeps operators in the results view.
Repeat searches to revisit earlier results
avg. 30
Each search step stays open as a tab.
Incident report after an investigation
manualAuto
Built from tracked subjects and their timeline.

Prototype test with 10 operators and stakeholders, Sep 2026. Average actions per task.

Problem

Scattered features left operators lost

Person-tracking features were spread across multiple screens, and every new search overwrote the previous results. As investigations grew longer, operators lost track of where they were and repeated searches to find results they had already seen.

Every new search resets my filters, so I have to start over.Security manager, enterprise client

I waste a lot of time switching between cameras to compare several people.User of a competing VMS

During a long search, I can't tell where I am.User of a competing VMS

Writing the report separately after the investigation is inefficient.Security manager, enterprise client

  • NavigationToo much screen switchingSearch and review meant constant jumps between screens.
  • IANo clear path to resultsObject details and analysis tools lived on separate screens.
  • JourneyData collected twiceSearch and reporting were split, so findings were gathered again.
Process

Prototype first, then specify

Screens and documents alone left room for misunderstanding, which surfaced only during build. After defining the structure, I built working prototypes with AI and reviewed them with engineering before writing the UI spec. Each round refined the layout and interactions before any production code existed.

Before
Research→Structure→Visual design→UI spec→Build↺ rework found mid-build
After
Research→Structure→AI prototype→Dev review→Visual design→UI spec→Build
Solution
Structure

Search, results and preview in one view

Operators set criteria, compare results and check original footage without leaving the screen.

  • Left: filters in one place, with criteria per subject type
  • Centre: results as a card list for side-by-side comparison
  • Right: original footage while the list stays in view
Workspace

Video, map and analysis connected

CCTV footage sits next to the movement path, nearby cameras and crowd data.

  • Virtual fence search within a drawn boundary
  • Heatmaps show crowd density at a glance
  • Adjacent and co-capturing cameras appear automatically
Comparison

Several people on one screen

Instead of switching between detail screens, operators add subjects to one view and compare footage and timelines side by side.

Reporting

Evidence flows into the incident report

Tracking results become an incident with paths and video evidence already linked, so the report is built from what was collected.

Learning

A prototype is a tool for testing hypotheses and aligning direction, not a preview of the output.

Documents alone could not build a shared picture of the screens and flows. Turning requirements into something stakeholders could click let us review direction weeks earlier.

Case 2 · Samsung SDS Cello Square

Freight Quote Redesign

Cello Square is Samsung SDS's logistics platform where business customers, from individual shippers to global companies, compare rates, request quotes and book shipments. I redesigned a fragmented quoting process into one connected journey from search to booking.

My role
  • Diagnosed issues through process analysis
  • Set the UX strategy
  • Designed wireframes and detailed UI
Team
2 designers · 3 engineers · 1 PM
Timeline
Mar – Dec 2025
Platform
Responsive web, desktop and mobile
Tags
Booking & checkoutBusiness customersSelf-service
Outcome

Duplicate input removed, one quote request flow

Quote entry points
41
Scattered entry points merged into rate search.
Clicks from rate search to submitted request
3319
Results link straight to the request: 42% fewer clicks.
Average re-quotes per quote
32
Auto-filled conditions and input guides: 33% fewer.

Clicks: task analysis, FCL ocean freight Busan → LA, 1 press or selection = 1 click. Re-quotes: Samsung SDS operational data, Dec 2025.

Problem

Scattered entry points left customers lost

Quote search and request were spread across screens and paths, so customers struggled to know the next step or their status. Similar-looking screens and repeated input raised the risk of drop-off.

  • Problem 1Four entry pointsFour quote entry points on the dashboard made it unclear where to start.
  • Problem 2Disconnected requestRate search and quote request were separate screens.
  • Problem 3Look-alike screensQuote status and booking shared layouts and were hard to tell apart.
Process

Mapping the as-is flow to find the breaks

I mapped every path from the dashboard to booking and marked where customers dropped off. The map showed two request screens split only by whether a rate existed, and four entry points that all led to the same search.

To-be
Rate search→Rate results→Quote request→Final review→Booking
Solution
Results

Compare rates at a glance, details on demand

I rebuilt the text-heavy results as rate cards. Origin, destination, rate and validity sit in the same place on every card, and the cost breakdown expands when needed.

Request

Step-by-step input with a live summary

The request is split into steps with the estimated cost pinned in a summary panel. Incoterms are explained with a diagram of each transport leg and who pays for it.

Handoff

Self-service first, a person when needed

Some shipments, such as dangerous goods, cannot be priced instantly. Instead of a dead end, the customer submits the same request and the operations team replies within two business days, with everything already entered.

  • Clear status and expected response time
  • No re-entry when the request moves to an agent
  • Same flow on mobile web
Learning

In complex B2B work, design the workflow before the features.

Prioritise within constraints

Fixed procedures meant screens could not change freely. I started where the workflow broke most often.

Design for the whole journey

Putting features on one screen did not simplify the work. They had to follow the order in which customers decide.

Case 3 · Samsung.com Global

Product Category Page Redesign

The product category page (PCD) is where shoppers browse and compare a category before choosing a product. Each business division built it differently, so the experience changed from category to category. I redesigned its structure so shoppers find and compare products more easily.

My role
  • Analysed navigation and user journeys
  • Defined the IA and UX strategy
  • Designed key screens, UX and UI
Team
3 designers · 1 engineer · 1 PM
Timeline
Jun – Dec 2024
Platform
Responsive web, desktop and mobile
Tags
B2CE-commerceSearch & discovery
Outcome

Less confusion, easier comparison

Page structures across divisions
per division1
One shared template for every division.
Scroll-to-bottom rate, MX page
avg. 33%55%
Condensed sections, key information only.
Specs shown per product
avg. 84
Only the essentials, to ease comparison.

Scroll data: MX (Mobile) PCD operational data, Jan 2025, compared with the division average. Spec count: design baseline.

Problem

Four discovery problems

  • DataAttention stays at the topFew shoppers reached product detail or checkout.
  • ComparisonA different page per divisionShoppers had to relearn each category.
  • ComponentsComponents ignore contentComponent choice did not match the information.
  • JourneyUnclear role per stageRepeated information tired shoppers before they compared.
Process

Heatmaps and page audits set the priorities

I compared scroll and click heatmaps across the Mobile, TV and Appliances divisions, then audited each page section by section to label its role. Most attention ended in the first screens, and similar content sat in different places on each page.

Solution
Entry

Category visuals and key information first

Product families are recognisable by image and name, and the hero sets a clear starting point on desktop and mobile.

Line-up

Line-ups and content in one flow

Product cards let shoppers scan families quickly, and content below expands on each family.

Compare

Key info first, detailed specs second

Image, colour, storage and price sit side by side. Specs follow in the same order, with Buy now and Learn more inside the comparison.

Learning

Design hierarchy and context before screens.

Data sets the priorities

Drop-off data, not opinions about the page, decided what to fix first.

Shared structure, product needs

A common template still needed room for differences between products and markets.
